derivations.claim: Fix one centered variable $Z$ with $|Z|\le b$ and let $\sigma^2=\mathbb E[Z^2]$. For every integer $k\ge2$, $|\mathbb E[Z^k]|\le\mathbb E[|Z|^k]\le b^{k-2}\sigma^2$. For fixed real $\lambda$, the exponential series converges uniformly on $[-b,b]$: its tail is bounded by $\sum_{k>N}(|\lambda|b)^k/k!\to0$. Thus finite linearity [F2] and the uniform tail bound permit termwise expectation in [F3], and the centered first-order term vanishes.

For $k\ge2$, $k!\ge2\cdot3^{k-2}$, by induction from $2!=2$ and the fact that each next factor is at least $3$. If $|\lambda|b<3$, [F3] and step 1.1 therefore give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z}\le1+\sigma^2\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{|\lambda|^k b^{k-2}}{k!}\le1+\frac{\lambda^2\sigma^2}{2(1-|\lambda|b/3)}\le\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2\sigma^2}{2(1-|\lambda|b/3)}\right),$ where the last inequality follows from $1+x\le e^x$ for $x\ge0$, which follows termwise from [F3].

For $0<\lambda<3/b$, repeated use of [F4] gives $e^{\lambda S_m}=\prod_{i=1}^m e^{\lambda Z_i}$. The factors are nonnegative measurable functions of the independent variables, so [F5] and step 2.1 yield $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S_m}=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z_i}\le\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2V}{2(1-\lambda b/3)}\right).$

If $V>0$, take $\lambda=t/(V+bt/3)$; then $0<\lambda b/3=bt/(3V+bt)<1$. On $\{S_m\ge t\}$, $e^{\lambda S_m}\ge e^{\lambda t}$. Markov [F6] and step 3.1 give $\mathbb P(S_m\ge t)\le\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2V}{2(1-\lambda b/3)}-\lambda t\right)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(V+bt/3)}\right).$

Applying step 4.1 to $-Z_1,\ldots,-Z_m$ gives the lower-tail bound, since this family remains independent, centered, bounded by $b$, and has the same total second moment $V$. If $V=0$, each nonnegative $Z_i^2$ has expectation zero, so [F7] makes every $Z_i=0$ almost surely; their finite sum is then zero almost surely.

derivations.claim: Define $k(\theta,x)=p_0(x)\log(p_0(x)/p_\theta(x))$ as $0$ when $p_0=0$ and as $+\infty$ when $p_0>0,p_\theta=0$. The sets $\{p_0=0\}$, $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$, and $\{p_0>0,p_\theta>0\}$ are product-measurable; on the last set the logarithm is a difference of measurable logarithms by [F13]–[F14]. Thus $k^+$ and $k^-$ are product-measurable by [F10]. Where $p_\theta>p_0>0$, setting $u=p_0/p_\theta\in(0,1)$ gives $-u\log u\le1/e$, so $k^-\le p_\theta/e$ and $\int k^-d\mu\le1/e$. If $P_0\ll P_\theta$, then $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}=0$; [F17] gives $p_0=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere there. Consequently, for every measurable $A$, the function $r_\theta=p_0/p_\theta$ on $\{p_\theta>0\}$ and $0$ otherwise satisfies $\int_A r_\theta\,dP_\theta=\int_{A\cap\{p_\theta>0\}}p_0d\mu=P_0(A)$. By [F18], it is a Radon–Nikodym derivative, so [F3] identifies $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)=\int k(\theta,x)d\mu$. Conversely, if $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}=0$, then every $P_\theta$-null set $A$ has $p_\theta=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, hence $P_0(A)=0$; thus failure of $P_0\ll P_\theta$ implies $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}>0$. In that case the same integral is $+\infty$, again equal to [F3]. Finally, Tonelli [F4] makes the integrals of $k^+$ and $k^-$ measurable in $\theta$; the latter is finite, so their difference gives a measurable extended-real KL map. For the log-square coordinate, the specified ratio conventions and [F10], [F13], [F14] give a nonnegative product-measurable integrand, whose section integral is measurable by [F4]. Hence $K_n\in\mathcal T$.

Set $Y_{\theta,i}:=p_\theta(X_i)/p_0(X_i)$ when $p_0(X_i)>0$ and $0$ otherwise. This is a measurable function of $X_i$ by [F10, F14]. Since $P_0\{p_0=0\}=\int_{\{p_0=0\}}p_0\,d\mu=0$, change of density using [F1, F2] gives $\mathbb E_{P_0}Y_{\theta,i}=\int_{\{p_0>0\}}p_\theta\,d\mu\le1$. For each fixed $\theta$, the $Y_{\theta,i}$ are independent measurable transforms of the IID coordinates; [F6, F7, F12] therefore give $\mathbb E_{P_0^n}\prod_iY_{\theta,i}\le1$. Joint measurability and Tonelli [F4] imply $\mathbb E_{P_0^n}D_n\le1$, so [F15] gives $D_n<\infty$ almost surely.

By [A1, F3], every $\theta\in K_n$ satisfies $P_0\ll P_\theta$, so $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}=0$. For each fixed $\theta$, the IID sample therefore has $\prod_i p_\theta(X_i)>0$ almost surely. Apply Tonelli [F4] to the zero-product indicator on $K_n\times\mathsf X^n$ with the product of the prior conditioned on K_n and the n-fold sampling law: for $P_0^n$-almost every sample, the conditional prior measure of parameters with zero product is zero. Hence the product likelihood is positive for prior-almost every $\theta\in K_n$, and [F17] implies its integral over the positive-mass set $K_n$ is positive. On the full-probability event where each $p_0(X_i)>0$, this implies $D_n>0$.

Write $\bar\Pi_n=\Pi(\cdot\mid K_n)$ and $\ell_\theta(x)=\log(p_\theta(x)/p_0(x))$ on the $P_0$-full set where both densities are positive. Put $Z(x)=\int\ell_\theta(x)\,\bar\Pi_n(d\theta)$. The KL and second-moment bounds in $K_n$, Tonelli [F4] applied to positive and negative parts, and [F3] give $\mathbb E_{P_0}Z(X_1)\ge-\epsilon_n^2$. Jensen [F5] for $z\mapsto z^2$ and [F4] give $\mathbb E_{P_0}Z(X_1)^2\le\int_{K_n}\mathbb E_{P_0}\ell_\theta(X_1)^2\,\bar\Pi_n(d\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2$.

Set $Z_i:=Z(X_i)$. By [F6] and [F7], the $Z_i$ are IID; [F8] and step 1.4 imply $\operatorname{Var}(Z_i)\le\epsilon_n^2$, so the centered variables are square-integrable and integrable. For $i\ne j$, the centered variables are independent measurable transforms of independent coordinates, so [F12] factors their product expectation and their covariance is zero. Applying [F11] to their finite sum therefore gives $\operatorname{Var}(n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i)=n^{-2}\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(Z_i)\le\epsilon_n^2/n$.

The mean of $n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i$ is at least $-\epsilon_n^2$ and its variance is at most $\epsilon_n^2/n$, by independence in step 2.1. Thus the event $n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i<-2\epsilon_n^2$ forces a deviation from its mean of at least $\epsilon_n^2$. Chebyshev [F9] yields $P_0^n\!\left\{n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i<-2\epsilon_n^2\right\}\le\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$

By Tonelli [F4] and the local second-moment bound, for $P_0^n$-almost every sample each of the finitely many functions $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta(X_i)$ is square-integrable under $\bar\Pi_n$; Cauchy–Schwarz [F16] makes their sum integrable. Step 1.2 bounds the integrated exponential by the finite $D_n/\Pi(K_n)$, so Jensen [F5] applies to that sum and the exponential. On the complementary event, it gives $D_n\ge\Pi(K_n)\int\exp\!\left(\sum_i\ell_\theta(X_i)\right)\bar\Pi_n(d\theta)\ge\Pi(K_n)\exp\!\left(\sum_iZ_i\right)\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}.$ Combining with step 3.1 proves the probability bound.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

If $P=Q$, then [F6] gives $\int_Ag\,d\mu=P(A)-Q(A)=0$ for every measurable $A$. For each integer $m\ge1$, on $E_m:=\{g\ge1/m\}$ we have $g\ge0$, so $0=\int_{E_m}g\,d\mu\ge\mu(E_m)/m$ and $\mu(E_m)=0$. Applying the same argument to $-g$ shows $\mu(\{g\le-1/m\})=0$. Since $\{g\ne0\}$ is the countable union of these null sets, $p=q$ almost everywhere and $h(P,Q)=0$. Thus $h$ is a metric on these laws.

Put $g:=p-q$ and $A:=\{x:g(x)\ge0\}$. Since $\int g\,d\mu=0$, the positive and negative parts have equal integral, so $\int_Ag\,d\mu=\frac12\int|g|\,d\mu$. For every measurable $B$, positivity of $g$ on $A$ and nonpositivity on $A^c$ give $\int_{A^c}g\le\int_Bg\le\int_Ag$; equality in the absolute supremum is attained at $A$ (or $A^c$). Thus [F4] gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\frac12d_1(P,Q)$.

Pointwise, if $p\ge q$ then $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p-q$, because $0\le(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)/(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\le1$ when the denominator is positive; the case $q\ge p$ is symmetric, and when both vanish the inequality is zero on both sides. Integrating and using [F1] yields $h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)$.

Factor $|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)$. By [F3], $d_1(P,Q)\le h(P,Q)\lVert\sqrt p+\sqrt q\rVert_2$. Also $\lVert\sqrt p+\sqrt q\rVert_2^2=2+2\int\sqrt{pq}\,d\mu\le4$, again by [F3] and the unit $L^2$ norms. Hence $d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q)$, and step 1.2 gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}\le h(P,Q)$.

They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

If $V=0$, then $S_m=0$ almost surely.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then

2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then

conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Choose one metric $d$ for both the entropy and conclusion: the root-L2 Hellinger distance $h$ of [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]], the full density distance $d_1(p,q)=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$, or the density distance $d_2(p,q)=(\int|p-q|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$. Its uniform prior mass is $2c\epsilon_n/(b-a)$. Since $-\log\epsilon_n=\frac12\log n+O(\log\log n)$ while $n\epsilon_n^2=4\log n$, there is a fixed $C>0$ such that this mass is at least $e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for large $n$.
